abstract: Oxford Nanopore direct RNA sequencing (dRNA-seq) reads native RNA molecules, and its basecaller now includes models that detect RNA modifications directly, among them inosine, the product of adenosine-to-inosine (A-to-I) editing by ADAR enzymes. These models are increasingly used, but how reliably they detect modifications in biological samples has rarely been tested. We evaluated the Dorado inosine model in a mouse macrophage cell line, comparing wild-type cells with ADAR1-knockout cells and in vitro transcribed RNA, before and after an inflammatory stimulus that increases editing. As a reference, we used the editing sites identified by Illumina sequencing of the same cells. We assessed whether the model distinguishes edited from unedited RNA, which negative control is needed to identify editing sites, how many reference sites are recovered, and why sites are missed. The confidence of the Nanopore inosine model alone was not sufficient to identify editing, and a matched ADAR-deficient control was essential. Even with this control, detection was limited by sequencing depth, by low editing levels and by basecalling errors at edited positions. Nanopore sequencing can detect A-to-I editing, but its inosine calls require an ADAR-deficient control and sufficient depth, and should be confirmed by an orthogonal method.
